title: Sliding Window Extremes with a Monotonic Deque
summary: Maintaining a sliding window's maximum or minimum in O(1) amortized time per step using a deque of indices kept in monotonic order, instead of rescanning the window.

slides.markdown:
Sliding Window Maximum asks for the max of every K-length window as it slides across an array. A [fixed-size window](fixed-size-sliding-window) usually maintains its aggregate with subtract-then-add, but max isn't reversible that way — if the outgoing element was the max, there's no O(1) way to recover the new max from a single running value.

The fix is a **monotonic deque**: a double-ended queue of array indices, kept in an order where the corresponding values strictly decrease from front to back. The front of the deque is always the current window's maximum. This is the last technique in the group, and it closes the loop back to a structure covered elsewhere — the deque's own push/pop mechanics are stack-and-queue fundamentals; this topic is specifically about applying them to windowing.

slides.subTitle: Keep indices whose values decrease front-to-back
slides.markdown:
The deque stores **indices**, not values, and maintains one invariant: `arr[deque[0]] >= arr[deque[1]] >= ... >= arr[deque[-1]]` — strictly decreasing values, front to back.

When a new index `i` arrives, pop from the **back** any index whose value is `<= arr[i]` before pushing `i` on. The reasoning: if `arr[i]` is at least as large as some earlier-but-still-in-window value, that earlier value can never be the max again for the rest of its time in the window — `arr[i]` is both larger (or equal) and will outlast it, since `i` is a later index. So those smaller trailing values are permanently useless and can be discarded.

This is a **greedy exchange argument** again, same flavor as the height-array topic earlier in this group — proving a discarded candidate can never win before throwing it away.

slides.sectionTitle: Deque contents as the window slides
slides.markdown:
For `arr = [1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7]`, `k = 3`: processing index 0 (value 1) pushes it — deque `[0]`. Index 1 (value 3): 3 >= arr[0]=1, so pop 0, push 1 — deque `[1]`. Index 2 (value -1): -1 < arr[1]=3, so just push — deque `[1, 2]`. Window max for indices 0-2 is `arr[1] = 3`, read from the front.

slides.sectionTitle: Sliding Window Maximum with a monotonic deque

slides.markdown:
A common bug: pushing `arr[i]` onto the deque instead of `i` itself. Everything about maintaining the decreasing-value order still works — but the window-expiry check (`dq[0] <= i - k`, "has the front fallen out of the window") becomes impossible, because a raw value carries no information about *which position* it came from.

If two different positions happen to hold equal values, storing values alone can't distinguish "this specific occurrence has aged out of the window" from "a different occurrence of the same value is still valid." Indices are unique and monotonically increasing by construction, which is exactly what makes the expiry check a clean, unambiguous comparison. Store indices; look up `arr[index]` only when you need the actual value for a comparison.

slides.sectionTitle: Popping from the front once the window outgrows the oldest index
slides.markdown:
The back of the deque handles "is this candidate ever going to matter"; the front handles a separate question — "has the current maximum aged out of the window." These are two different checks and easy to conflate.

The front-expiry check, `dq[0] <= i - k`, compares the *oldest surviving index* against the window's left boundary (`i - k + 1` is the window's left edge, so an index at or before `i - k` has already fallen out). This check has to run on every iteration, not just when a new max is pushed — an index can sit at the front, valid, for many steps, and then age out on a step where nothing was popped from the back at all. Skipping this check, or running it conditionally only when the back was just modified, is a common source of returning a stale maximum that's no longer actually inside the window.

slides.sectionTitle: Monotonic deque vs a heap for window max
slides.subTitle: O(n) amortized vs O(n log k)
slides.markdown:
A max-heap (of value, index pairs) is the other standard approach: push every element as it enters, pop from the top whenever the top's index has aged out of the window, and peek for the current max.

| | Monotonic deque | Max-heap |
|---|---|---|
| Time | O(n) amortized — each index pushed and popped at most once | O(n log k) — each push/pop is O(log k) |
| Space | O(k) worst case | O(n) worst case, since stale entries aren't removed until they reach the top |
| Expiry handling | Explicit check against the front index | Lazy deletion — stale tops are popped only when encountered |

The deque wins on both time and space here because it actively discards useless candidates from the back immediately, rather than letting a heap accumulate entries that might never be looked at again. The heap approach is worth naming as the more "generic" tool — one that generalizes to problems where the monotonic-order trick doesn't apply — but for pure sliding-window max/min, the deque is strictly better.

It's worth separating two layers of knowledge here. The **deque itself** — a double-ended queue supporting O(1) push and pop from both ends — is a plain data-structure fundamental, the same structure used for BFS level tracking, LRU caches, and general stack/queue problems, and its own push/pop mechanics belong to the study of stacks and queues broadly, not to this group specifically.

What's specific to this group is the **application**: using that structure to maintain a monotonic invariant over a sliding window so that the front is always the current extreme. The deque doesn't know or care that it's being used for windowing — the windowing logic (expiry checks against `i - k`, the amortized argument that each index is touched at most twice) is the part this topic owns.

When an interviewer asks you to implement this from scratch, being able to say "I'll use a deque here because it supports O(1) operations at both ends, which this invariant needs" — rather than just reaching for `collections.deque` by habit — signals you understand why the structure fits, not just that it does.

slides.sectionTitle: Why this is O(n) despite the nested-looking pops
slides.markdown:
The back-popping `while` loop inside the main `for` loop looks like it could make this O(n²) in the worst case — what if every new element pops the entire deque? The amortized argument resolves this the same way it did for the [variable-size window](variable-size-sliding-window): **every index is pushed onto the deque exactly once and popped at most once**, across the *entire* run, regardless of how the pops are distributed across iterations.

So even though a single iteration could pop many elements at once (if the array is, say, strictly decreasing then jumps to a new max), the total number of pop operations summed over the whole algorithm cannot exceed the total number of pushes, which is n. Total work is O(n) pushes plus O(n) pops, both bounded by n, giving O(n) overall — not O(n) per iteration times n iterations.

This group is built from two related but distinct engines. **Converging pointers** — opposite ends closing in, two sequences advancing whichever side is behind, same-direction compaction, kSum's fixed-and-converge, greedy height-array proofs — all justified by an invariant that lets you provably discard one side. **Sliding windows** — fixed-width edge updates, variable-width expand-and-shrink, hashmap-backed pattern matching, and this topic's monotonic deque for extremes — all justified by maintaining an incrementally updatable summary of a contiguous range instead of recomputing it.

The unifying interview skill across both: before writing any code, name the specific invariant or exchange argument that makes an O(n) or O(n²) pass sufficient, rather than pattern-matching on "there are two pointers" or "there's a window." That's what turns nine separate memorized solutions into one flexible technique.
